questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Allied plans for liberated Europe
questions.learningObjective: Explain how occupation zones were used to shape postwar Europe
questions.stem: In the translator's notes, a passage explains how the victorious powers divided Germany and Austria into zones before drawing up any constitution for them.

options.text: The zones were drawn along existing trade routes so that each power could export cheaply.
options.misconception: explains occupation zones by commercial convenience

options.text: The zones were temporary arrest lines, with no intention to govern from them afterwards.
options.misconception: treats zones as merely temporary checkpoints

options.text: The zones were fixed proportions of territory under military administration before political settlement.
The zones were arranged so that no single power held a majority of the occupied territory.
options.misconception: assumes the zonal map was designed for balance

questions.explanation: Dividing a country into occupation zones before writing any constitution fixes military control first. Political settlement was expected to follow the military map, which is why the zones mattered so much to the argument.
questions.hint: Note what came before constitution-making.

questions.stem: The translator's note on page forty records how Soviet forces stayed in eastern Europe and reshaped the governments they found.

options.text: Soviet forces withdrew quickly because the occupation was intended to be brief and temporary.
options.misconception: assumes a short Soviet presence in the east

options.text: Soviet forces stayed long enough to install friendly governments and tie them closely to Moscow.
Soviet forces stayed only because their supply lines required the local railway network.
options.misconception: reduces the presence to logistics

options.text: Soviet forces stayed to protect local Jewish communities from the violence of the period.
options.misconception: invents a humanitarian mission for the occupation

questions.explanation: Where forces remained for years, local leaders could be replaced, police forces reshaped and economies redirected towards Moscow. Duration itself created the alignment it is said to have merely found.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A railway that became a sovereignty test
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a sequence of stages in a contested railway
questions.stem: A translator's table lists four stages in a railway dispute: construction by foreign engineers, control by one power, wartime occupation of the line, and a post-war treaty ceding the assets.

options.text: The stages show that a railway never affected sovereignty, only the transport of goods.
options.misconception: denies the political role of infrastructure

options.text: The stages show that the line changed hands most often during the war years.
options.misconception: counts handovers without checking the dates

options.text: The stages show that the railway was settled permanently at the very first handover.
options.misconception: assumes an early permanent settlement

options.text: The stages show that control of the line was used to test sovereignty and finally settled by treaty.

questions.explanation: The sequence moves from construction to contested control to a treaty settlement, which is how a transport asset becomes a test of sovereignty. Counting handovers alone misses where the dispute was legally closed.
questions.hint: Look at the stage that ends the sequence.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The lesson drawn from the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the failures of the 1930s shaped postwar institutions
questions.stem: The translator's note records that a delegation was asked why the powers had failed to act in the 1930s and what had changed by the late 1940s.

answer.exemplar: The 1930s had shown that aggression met by conciliation was rewarded. When states defended one another through a collective mechanism that lacked an army, an aggressor could step in repeatedly without facing a military risk, and the eventual war arrived later and on a far greater scale. The lesson drawn afterwards was that agreement and enforcement had to be built before the crisis, not after it. That is why the late 1940s produced a permanent security council, an economic recovery programme and early-warning arrangements in atomic matters, all intended to remove the conditions that had made the earlier decade so dangerous.

questions.explanation: The note asks why the earlier decade was mishandled and what changed, so the answer must link the failure of collective action to the new institutions. Saying appeasement was wrong is not an explanation.
questions.hint: Link the earlier failure to the later institutions.

Aid was released automatically, so no power in the programme exercised any influence.
options.misconception: reads instalments as lack of influence

options.misconception: assumes a military purpose the circular does not state

options.text: Aid was meant to be spent on raw materials alone, so that recipient states kept their manufacturing.
options.misconception: invents a narrow spending restriction

questions.explanation: Quarterly instalments against reports are conditions attached to money, the ordinary way aid becomes leverage. Nothing in the circular supports a purely military purpose or uncontrolled distribution.
questions.hint: Note the conditions attached to the payments.

options.misconception: invents a rejection reason

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Soviet occupation and eastern alignment
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an occupation became a permanent political alignment
questions.stem: Marginal in the translator's notes, a passage asks for an account of how an occupation became a permanent political alignment in eastern Europe.

answer.exemplar: The alignment was produced less by propaganda than by control of the instruments of state. Soviet personnel remained in place, and in several countries opposition parties were banned or pushed out of the coalition governments. Land reform, nationalisation and the replacement of the old administrative elite created a new class of party functionaries whose careers depended on the new arrangement. Local elections were held with a single approved list, so the ballot confirmed rather than chose. Economically, the region was tied to Moscow by clearing agreements, joint ventures and preferential trade terms, and the western currency plan for Europe was presented to eastern governments as an unacceptable intrusion on their sovereignty. In the years that followed, the pattern of one-party rule and outside patronage hardened into the alignment that later divided Europe in two.

questions.explanation: The passage asks for a process, so the answer must show how control of institutions, parties and trade produced alignment rather than asserting it. Treating the outcome as one decision misses the mechanism.
questions.hint: Follow the institutions that were taken over.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Non-recognition of the new Chinese government
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequences of a policy of non-recognition
questions.stem: A translator's note asks for an account of how one government's refusal to recognise another shaped the diplomacy of the following decade.

answer.exemplar: The policy of non-recognition was meant to deny the new government the legitimacy that recognition conferred, and it was pursued through several instruments. Diplomatic missions stayed with the rival administration, assets were frozen, and American shipping and trade were restricted so that the new government could not easily be financed from abroad. The refusal was taken to the United Nations to keep a permanent seat occupied by a delegation the west did not accept. At the same time, aid and military ties with the island administration in the straits were expanded, turning a diplomatic position into a long-running commitment with its own costs, including a war that began in the same straits in 1950.

questions.explanation: The note asks for consequences, so the answer must connect the refusal to frozen assets, trade restrictions and the United Nations seat. Ending with the military dimension shows the policy carried costs.
questions.hint: List the instruments, not just the intention.

questions.explanation: Elections as soon as practicable and a supervising authority point away from preserving the old government and towards replacing it. Supervision remained, so direct rule by the victors does not fit either.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Aid to Greece and Turkey in 1947
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a bilateral request became a general policy of support
questions.stem: In the translator's notes, an explanation is requested of how aid to one Mediterranean country became a statement of policy for the whole region.

answer.exemplar: The request concerned Greece, where a civil war was under way between a government supported by the west and insurgent forces aligned with the communist parties to the north. British troops had been sent in 1941 and had fought since, but Britain told Washington that it could no longer afford the commitment and asked for American help instead. The American response turned a request about money into a declaration of policy, stating that the United States would support free peoples resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures and would provide economic and military assistance where requested. Greece and Turkey were named in the same breath, and Turkey's inclusion reflected Soviet demands for influence over the straits that concerned American planners. The episode established a template that the recovery programme for Europe would follow in the same year.

questions.explanation: The passage asks how a bilateral request became a general policy, so the answer must show the announcement's wording and the pairing with Turkey. Linking the episode to the later recovery programme completes it.
questions.hint: Follow the wording of the announcement itself.

questions.learningObjective: Read concession data as evidence of contested control
questions.stem: A translator's table gives the four possible routes of a railway line through mountain country and the number of years each concession allowed before renewal.

options.text: The table shows that the route with the shortest concession was the one the state most wanted.
options.misconception: infers preference from concession length

options.text: The table shows that state control of a route required securing the longest and hardest concession.
The table shows that the routes differed mainly in the length of their mountain crossings.
options.misconception: misses the concession column that matters

options.text: The table shows that all four routes were of equal strategic value to the state concerned.
options.misconception: asserts equal value the table never compares

questions.explanation: A railway is a sovereignty question when a state's control of its own territory depends on which line it holds and for how long. Concession length and difficulty together measure the contest.
questions.hint: Read the two columns together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The lesson drawn from the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a specific 1930s failure was designed out of later policy
questions.stem: The translator's note records an argument that the policy of the late 1940s had been designed to avoid a specific failure of the 1930s.

answer.exemplar: The failure in question was the belief that a crisis could be settled by appeals to reason among leaders who had already decided that war was unthinkable. Nothing backed that belief, so each concession was met by a further demand, and each concession was read at home as a national humiliation that the government could not survive politically. By the time the arguments were exhausted the other side had remade the strategic position, and the war began over questions that had been settled by force rather than negotiation. The later generation of policy was designed with that sequence in mind: commitments made in writing, disputes referred to institutions rather than to speeches, resources set aside in advance for enforcing them, and pressure applied early enough that no single concession could be presented as a final surrender.

questions.explanation: The argument asks for one failure and its antidote, so the answer must name the earlier sequence and match each institutional feature to it. Vague references to the past will not do.
questions.hint: Name the earlier sequence step by step.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The Marshall Plan as an instrument of containment
questions.learningObjective: Read an objection to aid as evidence of how the aid was understood

options.text: The reply shows that the delegation wanted the aid but objected only to the way it was administered.

The reply shows that the delegation had not understood the purposes of the programme at all.
options.misconception: claims ignorance the text contradicts

questions.explanation: Objecting to obligations that limit independent action is an objection to the aid's political character. The programme was read as a form of external direction, not as money with paperwork.
questions.hint: Focus on the words about independent action.

options.misconception: ignores the weights the table records

options.text: The table shows that the smaller occupiers combined held fewer votes than any single large one.
options.misconception: claims a coalition majority the table contradicts

options.misconception: invented a sequence the table cannot support

questions.explanation: Weighted voting gave the largest occupiers an effective veto over decisions, which shaped how the supervising body actually functioned. Equal votes would have produced a very different council, so the weighting is crucial.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Soviet occupation and eastern alignment
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the eastern settlement was harder to reverse than the western
questions.stem: In the translator's notes, several debates are summarised, one on why the eastern part of Europe proved so much harder to reverse after the war.

answer.exemplar: The eastern settlements were built without the mechanisms that would have allowed anyone to undo them. Governments were installed and approved from outside, and no elections were held that might have replaced them; the existing parties were dissolved or pushed aside and new ones were formed under supervision. Once a single party held every office, there was no lawful route by which a population could express a different preference, and even a decision to leave the settlement would have meant accepting its illegality. The western zones had elections, competing parties and an economic programme that tied their recovery to institutions the participants themselves controlled, so change there could come through agreed channels. The difference in reversibility therefore rested less on ideology than on whether any institutional channel for lawful change had been allowed to exist.

questions.explanation: The passage asks why one region was harder to reverse, so the answer must identify the absence of lawful channels for change rather than motives. The closing contrast shows the difference was institutional, not ideological.
questions.hint: Ask how change could lawfully have come about.

questions.explanation: Two governments, one director each, and changes requiring written consent of both describe an unresolved division. A line managed in common stays a sovereignty question rather than a settled asset.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Non-recognition of the new Chinese government
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a permanent seat carried such political weight
questions.stem: The translator's note records a decision to bar the rival government's delegation from occupying a permanent seat and asks for an explanation of why that mattered.

answer.exemplar: A permanent seat was more than a seat. It gave a government standing to speak for its country in the organisation that the war had created, and it placed that government's representative at the table where questions of peace, trade and colonial questions were decided. A rival government denied that standing could not be present at the table at all, and the claim would have to be made from outside, as an observer rather than as a participant. That distinction shaped what each side could attempt in the following years, because an observer could be ignored and could not be bound by decisions taken without it. Keeping the seat occupied also became the point at which the dispute repeatedly returned, turning a diplomatic position into a standing question about the legal order of the postwar world.

questions.explanation: The note asks why a seating matter carried weight, so the answer must explain the standing a seat conveyed and how exclusion narrowed what could be attempted. The last point shows it was a structural obstacle.
questions.hint: Ask what a seat let a government do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Aid to Greece and Turkey in 1947
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1947 doctrine shaped later American foreign policy
questions.stem: In the translator's notes, one doctrine is analysed, showing how a policy announced in 1947 shaped American foreign policy for twenty years.

answer.exemplar: The announcement committed the United States to support peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures, and to supply economic and military assistance where requested. Two elements of that formula did most of the work. By naming subjugation rather than any specific aggressor, it made the commitment indefinite, so a government facing an internal insurgency could claim that the outside pressure was the one that mattered. By making assistance available on request to any government that asked, it also placed the decision about intervention in the hands of the government that needed it, which produced a close and often tense relationship with the recipient. The formula was subsequently used to justify support for governments whose conduct at home many in Washington disliked, and its durability is the measure of how successfully the doctrine was framed.

questions.explanation: The passage asks for the doctrine's lasting shape, so the answer must explain the two elements that made it flexible and repeatable. The closing point shows the cost as well as the reach.
questions.hint: Explain the wording that made it repeatable.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The lesson drawn from the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1930s shaped the design of postwar economic recovery
questions.stem: The translator's note describes an economic programme adopted after the second world war and asks what earlier experience shaped its design.

answer.exemplar: The programme was shaped by what the previous decade had shown about economic collapse. In the 1930s falling output and mass unemployment had weakened governments, discredited established parties and made extremist movements electorally plausible, and the resulting political catastrophe had followed within a few years. Economists who wanted to prevent a repetition therefore argued that recovery had to be large enough to be visible, quick enough to change expectations, and structured so that it strengthened institutions rather than weakened them. Recovery was therefore to be administered largely by the countries receiving it, financed in a way that spread the cost widely, and made conditional on the recipients cooperating with one another, since a system of competing national recoveries would have reproduced the divisions that had done the damage in the first place.

questions.explanation: The note asks how earlier experience shaped design, so the answer must connect economic collapse in the 1930s to the size, administration and conditions of the later programme. Listing features without the link is not enough.
questions.hint: Connect each design feature to the earlier decade.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The Marshall Plan as an instrument of containment
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the programme required cooperation among recipients

stimulus.body: An announcement of the European recovery programme states that participating governments will coordinate their commercial policies and exchange plans for the coming four years. It adds that the programme will be administered by a committee of the participating states.

questions.stem: A translator's note asks whose cooperation the sponsors of the recovery programme wanted, and why that mattered.

options.text: It was meant to bind the participating economies together so that recovery would not restore the divisions of the 1930s.
It was meant to create a single currency for the participating states in the first year of the programme.
options.misconception: invents a monetary union that was not created

options.text: It was meant to reduce administrative costs by giving one body authority over all national budgets.
options.misconception: invents a supranational budget authority

options.text: It was meant to ensure that every participating country received the same total of aid.
options.misconception: claims an equal allocation the arrangement never promised

questions.explanation: Coordinating commercial policy turns separate national recoveries into an interdependent set. The aim was to prevent a return to competing national blocs whose weakness had fuelled extremism.
questions.hint: Ask what divided the region in the 1930s.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Aid to Greece and Turkey in 1947
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two postwar instruments shared a common logic
questions.stem: In the translator's notes, one entry covers the security assistance to Greece and Turkey, and a second covers the recovery programme for Europe.

options.text: The two entries show that the security assistance was simply the first stage of the recovery programme.
options.misconception: treats separate instruments as one programme

options.text: The two entries show that the recovery programme was the more important of the two measures.
options.misconception: ranks the instruments without evidence

options.text: The two entries show two instruments aimed at different problems but sharing one logic of collective support.
The two entries show that the second programme was designed to replace and withdraw the first.
options.misconception: invents a repudiation between the two measures

questions.explanation: One answered a security emergency and the other an economic weakness, but both rested on the same reasoning about collective support. Reading them as rivals misses the assumption underneath.
questions.hint: Look for the reasoning both entries share.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the Chinese government lost in 1949
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of foreign aid in sustaining a government
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how an occupying power's money and advisers did not secure the loyalty of the government they had been supporting.

options.text: Because the money arrived too late in the year to be spent before the harvest was lost.
options.misconception: invents a timing problem not in evidence

options.text: Because aid bought weapons but could not repair a currency, an army or a land settlement.
Because the occupying power's advisers were considered foreign and were therefore resented.
options.misconception: reduces the failure to popular resentment of advisers

options.text: Because the government preferred fighting to the embarrassment of asking for more help.
options.misconception: invents a pride explanation for the government's choices

questions.explanation: External money can supply arms but not the domestic settlement on which an army's loyalty depends. Without pay and land, weapons and advisers were not enough to keep a state supplied.
questions.hint: Ask what loyalty in an army actually depends on.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Non-recognition of the new Chinese government
questions.learningObjective: Read recognition counts as evidence of the speed and unevenness of change
questions.stem: The translator's table lists, for the years after 1949, the number of governments that exchanged diplomatic missions with the new government, and the number that continued to deal with its rival.

options.text: The table shows that most governments exchanged missions with the new government within the first year.
options.misconception: reverses the counts the table records

options.text: The table shows that no government changed which rival it dealt with during the whole period.
options.misconception: ignores the changes the table records

options.text: The table shows that recognition spread steadily and evenly across the whole decade.
options.misconception: describes even spread the counts contradict

options.text: The table shows that recognition spread slowly and unevenly, with most states changing only much later.

questions.explanation: A slow, uneven spread with a long lag before most states moved is what a policy of exclusion produced. The counts show durability and gradualism, not rapid spread or isolation.
questions.hint: Look at the shape of the two columns over time.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Allied plans for liberated Europe
questions.learningObjective: Read voting weights as evidence of how a settlement would function
questions.stem: The translator's table lists the members of the council that supervised the liberated territories, and the number of votes each was allotted.

options.text: The table shows that every member had one vote, so decisions reflected the number of members present.
options.misconception: ignores the weights the table records

options.text: The table shows that the largest occupier was given more members but fewer votes than the others.
options.misconception: invents a members column the table does not contain

options.text: The table shows that the votes were split evenly so that no single member could decide anything.
options.misconception: claims an even split the weights contradict

options.text: The table shows that voting was weighted by size, giving the largest occupiers a standing veto.

questions.explanation: Weighted voting gave the largest occupiers an effective veto, which shaped how the supervising body functioned. Equal votes would have produced a very different council, so the weighting is crucial.
questions.hint: Read the votes column beside the names.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Soviet occupation and eastern alignment
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a region was reorganised around a new economic bloc
questions.stem: A translator's note on regional trade asks what the document shows about the character of the region's economic alignment.

answer.exemplar: The redirection was worked out by three steps that ran together. Politically, the communist parties took the leading positions in every eastern government and drove out the parties that might have organised opposition, so that the states' decisions could be made without a contest. Economically, an economic body was created to coordinate industrial targets and trade between the eastern states, with the production of steel, coal and machinery planned across the region rather than within each country. Finally the western recovery programme was refused, because accepting aid that came with conditions attached would have made eastern policy a continuation of the western programme rather than an alternative to it. The result was a region whose trade, investment and political authority all pointed in one direction, and whose economic life was harder to rejoin to the west than before the war.

questions.explanation: The note asks how a region was reorganised, so the answer must connect political control, economic planning and the refusal of western aid. Omitting the aid question leaves the bloc unexplained.
questions.hint: Cover politics, planning and the refused aid.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A railway that became a sovereignty test
questions.learningObjective: Read an engineering report as evidence of shared frontier sovereignty

stimulus.body: An engineering report of 1946 states that the line crosses a frontier twice between the two capitals. It notes that both crossings are fitted for railway gauge conversion and that the sidings at the border station are owned in equal shares by the two authorities.

questions.stem: A translator's note on railway gauges asks what the arrangement at the border station demonstrates.

options.text: The report demonstrates that the line had been surveyed by engineers of a third country.
options.misconception: infers third-country involvement from an engineering report

options.text: The report demonstrates that the two authorities had already agreed to abandon the line entirely.
options.misconception: reads shared ownership as an intention to abandon

options.text: The report demonstrates that even technical assets had been divided into shared sovereignty at the frontier.
The report demonstrates that the border crossing had been built to allow military trains to pass unchecked.
options.misconception: assumes a military purpose for the gauge facilities

questions.explanation: Shared ownership of border sidings shows the frontier cutting through infrastructure rather than infrastructure stopping at it. Where facilities are jointly held, sovereignty has to be negotiated in detail.
questions.hint: Look at who owns the sidings.

questions.topic: The lesson drawn from the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two postwar measures answered the same earlier lesson

options.text: The two entries show that the same policy was applied twice, once to a country and once to a continent.
options.misconception: treats different instruments as one policy

options.text: The two entries show that economic aid was preferred to military support in every case.

options.text: The two entries show different instruments answering different parts of the problem the earlier decade revealed.
The two entries show that the second programme was designed to undo the effects of the first.

questions.explanation: One instrument answered a security problem and the other an economic one, but both responded to the lesson that collapse produced extremism. Reading them as rival policies misses their shared purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what each instrument was aimed at.
